Row.Text: In 330 Constantine dedicated a new capital on the Bosporus, on the site of the old Greek colony of Byzantion. The city commanded the only sea passage between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea and the land road between Europe and Asia, and it was ringed by water on three sides. When the western provinces of the Roman Empire dissolved in the fifth century, the eastern half, governed from Constantinople, simply carried on. Its people called themselves Romans to the end; "Byzantine" is a name given to them by later historians.

Under Justinian (527-565) the empire briefly reconquered Italy, North Africa and southern Spain, codified Roman law, and raised the Hagia Sophia, whose dome was the largest in the world for nearly a thousand years. The Theodosian Walls, a triple line of fortifications built in the fifth century, turned back Avars, Arabs, Bulgars and Rus alike; the city was not taken by an enemy until the Fourth Crusade in 1204.

The seventh century brought catastrophe. Persia and then the Arab caliphate stripped away Syria, Egypt and the wealth that came with them, and the empire reorganised itself around the themes: provinces whose soldiers farmed the land they defended. The armoured cataphract and the fire-throwing dromon were the instruments of this smaller, harder state, and a famously patient diplomacy did the rest, playing neighbour against neighbour with gold, titles and marriages.

The Macedonian dynasty (867-1056) presided over a second flowering. Basil II broke Bulgaria, the frontier returned to the Danube and the Euphrates, missionaries carried the Cyrillic alphabet and Orthodox Christianity to the Slavs, and the city's workshops, scriptoria and the Hippodrome made Constantinople the largest and richest city in Christendom.

Decline came from the defeat at Manzikert in 1071, the loss of Anatolia to the Turks, and the sack of 1204, after which a restored but diminished empire held little more than the city and a few coasts. On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman army of Mehmed II breached the walls with cannon, and the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting. Byzantium's law, art, liturgy and imperial idea lived on in Russia, the Balkans and the Renaissance West.

The kataphraktos, the "fully armoured one", was the heavy cavalryman of the East Roman army: rider and horse alike wrapped in lamellar and mail, the man carrying a long kontos lance, a mace and a bow, the horse wearing a chamfron and a skirt of iron scales. The type came to Rome from its Iranian and Sarmatian enemies, and Byzantium kept it long after the western provinces had fallen.

Under the Macedonian emperors the cataphracts were reorganised into a wedge of several hundred riders that struck the centre of an enemy line while lighter horse worked the flanks. The tenth-century military manuals describe the formation in detail, and the armies of Nikephoros Phokas and Basil II used it to reconquer Crete, Antioch and Bulgaria. The word survives in every European language as the name for the heaviest cavalry.

The dromon, "the runner", was the standard warship of the Byzantine navy from the sixth to the twelfth century: a fast galley with one or two banks of oars, a lateen sail, a raised castle at the stern and a spur at the bow for breaking an enemy's oars. It replaced the ram-bowed galleys of antiquity, which needed heavier hulls than the empire could afford.

Its most feared weapon was Greek fire, a petroleum mixture pumped through a bronze siphon mounted in the bow and ignited as it left the tube. The recipe was a state secret. Fire-bearing dromons broke two Arab sieges of Constantinople, in 678 and 718, and turned back the Rus fleets of 941 and 1043; contemporaries said the ships breathed fire like dragons and that even water would not put it out.

The Hippodrome of Constantinople, laid out by Septimius Severus and completed by Constantine, was the largest building in the city: a U-shaped track some 450 metres long with tiered seats for perhaps a hundred thousand people. Down its centre ran the spina, decorated with trophies gathered from across the empire, including the Egyptian obelisk of Thutmose III and the bronze Serpent Column from Delphi.

It was far more than a racecourse. The emperor showed himself to the people from the kathisma, the imperial box connected directly to the palace; victories were celebrated there and rebels were executed there. The chariot factions, the Blues and the Greens, were political parties as much as fan clubs, and in 532 their combined riot, the Nika revolt, burned half the city before Justinian's generals ended it in the Hippodrome itself.

The Great Palace occupied the whole south-eastern tip of the peninsula, between the Hippodrome and the sea walls: not one building but a walled district of audience halls, churches, barracks, gardens and terraces descending to the Bosporus, built and rebuilt by emperors from Constantine to the Komnenoi. The bronze gate of the Chalke opened onto the Augustaion, the square before the Hagia Sophia.

Here the empire's diplomacy was staged. Ambassadors were led through courts and colonnades to the Magnaura, where the emperor sat enthroned beside golden lions that roared and a golden tree full of singing mechanical birds; the throne itself rose on a lift while the visitor prostrated himself. Constantine VII's Book of Ceremonies records every step. The point was to make the wealth and antiquity of Rome self-evident before a word was spoken.

The Augustaion was the ceremonial heart of Constantinople: a colonnaded square between the Hagia Sophia, the Senate house, the Baths of Zeuxippos and the Chalke gate of the Great Palace, with the Hippodrome a few steps away. Justinian raised a column at its centre bearing his own bronze equestrian statue, facing east with an orb in its hand. From the Milion arch beside it, all distances in the empire were measured.

Justinian's Church of the Holy Wisdom was built in less than six years, between 532 and 537, on the site of two earlier basilicas burned in riots. Its architects, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, were mathematicians rather than master builders, and their solution to setting a round dome over a square nave, four great pendentives carrying a dome 31 metres across, had never been attempted at that scale. Justinian is said to have entered the finished church and declared, "Solomon, I have outdone thee."

The first dome fell in an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt higher; the building has stood since, through more earthquakes, the sack of 1204, the conversion to a mosque in 1453 and its later life as a museum. For nine centuries it was the largest cathedral in the world, the coronation church of the emperors, and the model for Orthodox architecture from Kiev to the Balkans. Envoys of Vladimir of Kiev, sent to compare the religions of their neighbours, reported that inside it they "knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth."

After the Arab conquests of the seventh century stripped away Syria and Egypt, the empire reorganised what remained into themes: provinces governed by a general, whose soldiers were settled on the land and served in return for hereditary holdings rather than pay. The system turned Anatolia into a self-defending frontier and freed the treasury from the cost of a standing field army.

The themes gave Byzantium three centuries of resilience. Their soldiers held the Taurus passes against annual raids, their fleets in the Aegean and Carabisiani themes kept the sea lanes, and their generals, dangerously, became the emperors of the eighth and ninth centuries. The system decayed when landowners bought up soldiers' farms, and the professional tagmata of the capital took over the wars of reconquest.

The pentarchy was the idea that the universal Church was governed by five patriarchs, of Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, and that their consensus in council defined orthodoxy. Justinian gave the doctrine legal form. In practice the emperor summoned the councils, and Constantinople, the "New Rome", claimed second place after Old Rome, a claim that Rome never accepted.

Church and state were interlocked. The emperor was God's viceroy on earth and the patriarch crowned him in the Hagia Sophia; relics, icons and processions were instruments of policy as much as devotion, and the dispute over icons in the eighth and ninth centuries was fought as fiercely in the palace as in the monasteries. The break with Rome in 1054 confirmed a separate Orthodox world with Constantinople at its head.

Porphyrogennetos, "born in the purple", named a child born to a reigning emperor in the Porphyra, the purple-walled chamber of the Great Palace. The title marked legitimacy in a state whose throne was, in theory, open to anyone the army and people acclaimed, and where usurpation was common. A purple-born heir could expect loyalty that a general who had seized the crown could not.

The most famous holder, Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, spent a childhood in the shadow of his co-emperor Romanos Lekapenos and used the years to become the empire's great compiler: the Book of Ceremonies, the treatise On the Administration of the Empire written for his son, and an encyclopaedia of imperial knowledge. Under the Macedonian dynasty the dignity of the office, its ritual and its scholarship were as much a weapon as the army.

Byzantion was founded by Greek colonists from Megara around 657 BC on the European shore of the Bosporus, on a site the oracle at Delphi had pointed out: opposite the "city of the blind", Chalcedon, whose settlers had overlooked the better harbour. Its position on the grain route from the Black Sea made it rich and repeatedly besieged. Septimius Severus razed it in 196 and rebuilt it; Constantine chose it for his new capital in 324.

After 1453 the Byzantine inheritance was claimed on several sides. Moscow's rulers married into the Palaiologoi, took the double-headed eagle and the title of tsar, and called their city the Third Rome; the Ottoman sultans styled themselves Kayser-i Rum and governed from Constantinople with Byzantine ceremony. The Greek revival of the nineteenth century looked to Byzantium for its church, its script and its capital, an idea that shaped the Balkans until 1922.
